https://aeon.co/essays/knowledge-is-a-st.question: Is knowledge a necessary category for rational action, or does reliable belief do the work?
https://aeon.co/essays/knowledge-is-a-st.thesis: Papineau contends that our demand for knowledge beyond true belief can privilege seemingly direct evidence and obscure useful probabilistic evidence.
https://aeon.co/essays/knowledge-is-a-st.argument: A lucky true guess is not knowledge. Even a highly likely correct conclusion can fail ordinary knowledge intuitions. Papineau argues that practical action should track justified probability and consequences, not a separate label of knowledge.
https://aeon.co/essays/knowledge-is-a-st.intellectual_background: The essay engages epistemology's longstanding effort to distinguish knowledge from true belief, and applies the issue to evidence in courts and communication.
https://aeon.co/essays/knowledge-is-a-st.example: If 99 of 100 people participated in a riot but one did not, bare group statistics give a high probability of guilt yet may not justify convicting any particular defendant.
https://aeon.co/essays/knowledge-is-a-st.strongest_objection: Rejecting knowledge risks losing the protections that require evidence to connect a specific person with a particular act; aggregate probabilities alone can produce serious injustice.
https://aeon.co/essays/knowledge-is-a-st.possible_response: Papineau would focus on expected error costs and evidentiary quality rather than a categorical knowledge requirement, but this does not settle the moral asymmetry between wrongful conviction and acquittal.
https://aeon.co/essays/knowledge-is-a-st.implications: Decisions might be clearer if they state confidence, evidence type and costs of error.
unresolved_questions: Are knowledge standards a useful safeguard against statistical injustice?
When should practical action require more than high probability?
Can probability alone capture respect for individuals?
